extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, entertainment, and cancel-culture debates
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for judging comedians' past jokes, performances, and public controversies in the context of changing social norms and cancel-culture debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of racist performance and slurs
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic material should not include racist depictions or racial slurs (examples cited: wearing blackface, using racial epithets, minstrel references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites multiple examples from Sarah Silverman’s career — a 2007 sketch where she wore blackface, a 2010 tweet captioned “I’m having minstrel cramps,” and a 2001 TV joke using the racial slur “c—k” — as behavior that has drawn public criticism. These are presented as clear anti-patterns that attract sustained backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for past material
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers should acknowledge problematic past material and take responsibility for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silverman: “You have to be accountable.” The piece portrays accountability as a necessary response to controversial past work rather than denial or silence. Examples include publicly discussing past sketches and tweets and accepting critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of personal growth (cringing at old work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking back at old material with discomfort (cringing) is an indicator of growth rather than something to be ashamed of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silverman: “There’s so much in my first special that makes me cringe, but I’m not ashamed of it. You have to be accountable. And if you don’t look back at your old shit and cringe, you’re not growing.” The article frames cringing as a positive sign of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualizing material as 'from another time'
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess past comedy in light of the era in which it was created; earlier material may reflect norms that have since changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silverman notes: “It’s so from another time, and it’s interesting to have done comedy through such totally different times.” The piece suggests critics and audiences should factor historical context into evaluations of older work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique should allow for change rather than pure cancellation ('righteousness porn')
rubrics_metrics.description: When responding to offensive past behavior, criticism should be aimed at accountability and possible change, not only punitive expulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silverman criticizes a punitive, performative mode of response: “there’s this kind of ‘righteousness porn’ going on with canceling people over their past... with no earnest hope that they may be changed.” The article implies that productive critique seeks remediation or growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of historical analogies about repression
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overstating parallels between contemporary online shaming and historical repression without acknowledging scale and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silverman compares current criticism to a “mutated McCarthy era,” but the article notes the real McCarthy era involved imprisonment and mass job loss. Guidance: be precise and proportionate when invoking historical analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of a performer’s continued public success as part of evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedian's commercial success and institutional recognition (awards, specials, tours) complicate assessments of whether they have been or should be 'canceled.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece points to Dave Chappelle’s continued success — Netflix specials, sold-out tours, and receiving the Mark Twain Prize — as context that affects how criticism functions in practice and how consequences are perceived.
